subject: opportunity-cost
title: What You Give Up When You Choose
summary: Every choice has a hidden cost: the next-best thing you did not pick.

keys.answer: The value of the next-best thing you give up when you make a choice.

options.text: The next-best thing you give up when you choose
The price tag printed on a toy
Getting two things at once for free

keys.prompt: Why do we have to choose at all?
keys.answer: Because of scarcity: we want more than our time, money, and stuff can cover.

options.text: Wants are bigger than what we have (scarcity)
Choosing is only a game adults invent
There is always enough of everything

keys.prompt: If you pick one toy with your dollar, what is the opportunity cost?
keys.answer: The other toy you most wanted instead—not every toy in the store.

options.text: The other toy you most wanted instead
Every toy in the whole store
Nothing, if the dollar was a gift

cards.title: One dollar, two toys
cards.text: You have one dollar. Two toys each cost a dollar. You can buy only one. What did choosing cost you—besides the dollar?

cards.question: You buy the bear. What is the real "opportunity cost"?

options.text: The other toy you would have bought next
Every toy you saw in the store
Only the dollar you handed over

cards.reveal: Economists say opportunity cost is the next-best thing you give up—not every other option, and not just the price tag.

cards.title: Not enough of everything
cards.text: Scarcity means we want more than our time, money, and stuff can cover. Because of that, we have to choose.
cards.example: Say… you have one free afternoon. You cannot play soccer, practice golf, and build a whole fort at once.

cards.title: The next-best thing
cards.text: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative when you decide—it's what you give up. It is only that next-best choice, not every other idea you had.
cards.example: Say… you pick soccer practice over a movie. The opportunity cost is the movie you skipped, not also skipping a trip, a game, and a nap.

why.q: Why only the next-best thing, not every option?
why.a: You could only have done one other thing with that same time or money, so you give up the one you valued next.

examples_by_interest.golf: Say… you choose range time over a video game. The opportunity cost is the game session you skipped.
examples_by_interest.soccer: Say… you choose practice over a movie. The opportunity cost is the movie you skipped.
examples_by_interest.business: Say… you spend allowance on lemonade cups instead of stickers. The opportunity cost is the stickers you did not buy.

cards.title: Even "free" has a cost
cards.text: A free pizza still takes your lunchtime. You give up eating with friends somewhere else. Choice always brings an opportunity cost.
cards.example: Economists like Milton Friedman's line: there is no such thing as a free lunch—because choosing uses scarce time or stuff.

cards.title: Look for the hidden trade
cards.text: People often notice the price they pay and miss what else that time or money could have done. Asking "what else could I do?" makes the trade clearer.
cards.example: Say… before you buy a snack, ask what else that money could buy this week—or what else that ten minutes could be.

cards.question: Think of a choice you made this week. What was the next-best thing you gave up?
nudges: Was it time, money, or both?
Would a friend have picked a different next-best thing?

options.text: Wants are bigger than what we have
options.why: Yes. Limited time, money, and stuff force choices.

options.text: Stores never run out of toys
options.why: Scarcity is about not having enough for every want.

options.text: Choices never cost anything
The next-best thing you give up
options.why: Right. It is what you forgo when you choose.

options.text: Only the sticker price
options.why: Price is one cost; opportunity cost is the alternative you skip.

options.text: Getting both options at once
options.why: Opportunity cost appears because you cannot have both.

questions.q: You choose the park over the beach. What is the opportunity cost?

options.text: The beach trip you did not take
options.why: Yes—the next-best plan you gave up.

options.text: Every vacation on Earth
Nothing, because parks are free
options.why: Even free places use scarce time.

sources.title: Opportunity Cost (scarcity, choice, and "no free lunch")
sources.supports: Scarcity: wants greater than resources; choice is required; opportunity cost is the most highly valued opportunity given up (next-best only, not every option); free pizza still has an opportunity cost; Milton Friedman "no such thing as a free lunch."

sources.title: Real-Life Examples of Opportunity Cost
sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
sources.supports: Definition: opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative when a decision is made—what is given up; scarcity of time, money, and resources drives trade-offs.

sources.title: Opportunity cost
sources.supports: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone when a choice is made between mutually exclusive alternatives; not limited to money—time and other benefits count too.
